newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N., Pakistan envoys postpone Afghan peace trips.
newsitem.headline: U.N., Pakistan envoys postpone Afghan peace trips.

text.p: U.N. and Pakistani envoys put off peace trips to Afghanistan on Thursday as opposition leaders were unavailable for talks and there was bad weather in the south, U.N. and Pakistani officials said.
The opposition northern alliance fighting the Taleban Islamic militia postponed at the last minute talks with U.N. envoy Norbert Holl on a mission to head off a battle for the capital, Kabul.
U.N. officials in Mazar-i-Sharif said the talks were put off until Friday because alliance leaders were out of the northern city where the negotiations were to be held.

In Islamabad, a senior Pakistani Foreign Ministry official, Iftikhar Murshed, could not leave for the southern Afghan city of Kandahar for talks with Taleban officials because of the bad weather, a ministry spokesman said.
He said Murshed, seeking the warring factions' agreement on holding intra-Afghan dialogue proposed by Pakistan, would now go to Kandahar on Saturday.
Holl was informed of the postponement less than 12 hours before he was scheduled to fly to Mazar from Islamabad, U.N. officials told Reuters.

"We have been told that (opposition leader) General Abdul Malik and a delegate representing (ousted government's top military commander Ahmed Shah) Masood cannot be in Mazar on Thursday," the officials said. "The talks have been rescheduled for Friday."

The last-minute postponement added to speculation that a decisive battle was imminent between the alliance and the nominal Kabul government of Taleban, an Islamic fundamentalist grouping of mainly southern Afghan Pashtuns.

There were reports on Thursday in Mazar, the Afghan rebel headquarters, that the battle would not only be for Kabul but also for the western city of Herat, another Taleban stronghold that controls access to Iran, which supports the alliance.
Travellers just returned from the battle lines around Kabul said Masood had brought in nearly 1,000 more troops into his force and was ready for an attack on the capital at any moment.

Travellers just back from near Herat reported there were signs that Malik was massing troops in the area for a coordinated attack with Masood fighters on Herat, which the Taleban reinforced in recent days in anticipation of an attack.
"If the alliance captured Herat it would be almost as important strategically as Kabul, because the city controls key supply lines in Afghanistan," a U.N. source said.

With opposition forces poised less than 10 miles (16 km) from Kabul, within easy rocket and artillery range of the city, Holl's mission was regarded as a final chance to avert a new cycle of violence, which some analysts believe can lead to a de facto partition of Afghanistan into north and south.
The possible battle for Kabul puts the Taleban against a grouping of ethnic Uzbeks, Tajik and Hazaras who control the northern part of the country.

Holl's mission, described by U.N. sources in Mazar-i-Sharif as a fact-finding tour, is to prepare for a visit in about one week's time of U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan's newly appointed special envoy for Afghanistan, Lakhdar Brahimi.
